# Open Verbs {#sec-verbs}

Decapsulating methods is a bet that a domain is an algebra. The verbs are
the operations. The types are the elements they operate on. Extensibility
means a new element can join an old operation, or a new operation can be
defined on old elements, without anyone opening the type and adding a
method to its private table.

R made that bet early, because statistics is full of operations that apply
to more than one kind of thing: `print`, `plot`, `summary`, `predict`,
`coef`, `[`. A model object does not contain the verb `predict`. The verb
exists, and methods attach to it. Rust made a related bet for different
reasons, and the resemblance is real if you do not sand off the parts that
do not resemble.

## Generic functions

In the generic-function tradition, the operation is a function and the
method is chosen from the arguments. CLOS is the carefully designed
version: multi-argument dispatch, method combinations, classes that do
not own their behavior. S3 is the casually designed version that won: a
naming convention, a search along the class vector, first-argument
dispatch unless you reach for something richer. S4 adds formality and
multiple dispatch. S7 keeps S3's compatibility and adds a class and
property model worth using. [Advanced R's object-oriented
chapter](https://adv-r.hadley.nz/oo.html) sorts these without pretending
they are one system.

The user's daily experience of the bet:

- a new package implements `format.my_class` and the console changes
- a new package implements `predict.my_model` and old code starts working
- nobody subclasses the original type
- the verb stays a function, so it can sit in a pipe, a script, or a shell

Message-passing inverts the sentence. `obj.predict()` asks the object
which method to run. Discovery is "what does this object know?" Extension
is subclassing, wrapping, or patching. Python and JavaScript made this
the default and it fits simulation-shaped problems: widgets, game
entities, documents with a long identity, ORMs whose rows really are
handles. It fits data work only after you build a second, functional
layer on top and try not to talk about it.

R has both, and the culture never fully picked. R6 and reference classes
are the message-passing wing. S3/S4/S7 are the generic-function wing. The
winning user interfaces in statistics and in the tidyverse are still
`verb(noun)` or `noun |> verb()`. `$` exists. It is not a moral failure to
use it on a handle. It is a clue that you have built a handle.

## What Rust actually shares

Rust methods are sugar over functions. `value.method(args)` is
`Type::method(value, args)` or `Trait::method(value, args)`. There are
two places a method can come from:

- an **inherent** `impl Type` block, which is closed: only the crate that
  owns the type adds these
- a **trait** implementation, which is open in a controlled way: other
  crates can implement the trait for their own types

The
[traits chapter of the Rust book](https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch10-02-traits.html)
is the mechanism. The
[API guidelines](https://rust-lang.github.io/api-guidelines/) are the
culture: types carry invariants, traits carry shared behavior, and a lot
of the surface area of a good crate is functions. Ownership and lifetimes
have no R equivalent, and pretending otherwise is how the comparison gets
cute and then wrong. The comparison that holds is the shape of the code
you read. You navigate a vocabulary of functions. Types are the backbone
those functions accept. Dispatch is a property of the operation. A new
type can join `Display`, or `predict`, without editing the original
module.

Rust's orphan rules are the part R deliberately does not have. A trait
implementation has to be coherent: you cannot have two crates each
defining `Display` for the same foreign type and then wonder which one
runs. R will happily let the next attached package mask a method, and
`UseMethod` will pick whatever is found first on the search path. That is
the extensibility and the footgun in one rule. Packages manage it with
conventions, imports, and a refusal to define methods for classes they do
not own unless that is the whole point of the package. The footgun is not
an argument against open verbs. It is an argument for a curated
vocabulary, which is the same argument the naming section already made.

## Naming as the module system you actually use

Thinking in functions and shell-like procedures matches how you navigate
a codebase under this bet.

- `api_config_new`, `api_client_fetch`, `color_brightness`
- `check_*`, `as_*`, `format_*`, `req_*`
- Rust's `module::function`

The prefix is the module. The package namespace is the fence. IDE
navigation is symbol search over a vocabulary you chose, which is the
same muscle as a good CLI. Encapsulation, in this style, means three
things and refuses a fourth:

- **semantic:** illegal states do not parse
- **nominal:** the names are stable and the namespace is real
- **disciplinary:** effects and handles are obvious in the signature
- not: every verb hides behind `self.`

Dot-driven objects optimize for one blob of state with a toolbox
attached. Function-and-type systems optimize for pipelines, scripts, and
verbs that apply to more than one noun. Data work is the second shape.
So are HTTP clients, tool-using model loops, and compilers. When an R
codebase feels like Java with the classes rubbed off, it is usually
because the verbs were never written down as verbs. The methods exist,
scattered across files named after nouns, and the user interface is
whatever you discover by typing `$` and waiting.

## Algebras, not simulations

The cold version of the strength:

A simulation asks "what does this thing do next?" An algebra asks "what
operations exist on these things, and which laws do they obey?" R's
generic functions are a bet on the second question. So are Rust traits,
CLOS generic functions, and type classes in Haskell. Python's classes are
a bet on the first, with protocols and `functools.singledispatch` as the
escape hatches for people who wanted the second bet after all.

Your preference is not anti-object. It is objects as a facade over a
functional surface. Types carry meaning. Generics carry extensibility.
Functions are what humans, pipes, and shells invoke. That is a coherent
production style. It is one of the real reasons to stay in R when the
alternative is an object graph that can do anything and explains nothing.

The style has a failure mode worth naming. A vocabulary nobody curates
becomes a junk drawer of verbs: three ways to say "fetch," methods
defined for classes the package does not own, generics with a single
method that should have been a function. Open dispatch is valuable when
there is a second implementation in sight, or a stranger who might write
one. A private function is a fine verb. Not everything has to dispatch.
The test is whether a new noun should be able to join without editing the
call sites. If yes, write the generic. If no, write the function and keep
the name clean.
